title: Populations and Carrying Capacity
seo_title: Carrying Capacity Worksheets: Population Growth, Limiting Factors (High School Biology)
standard_text: Use mathematical and/or computational representations to support explanations of factors that affect carrying capacity of ecosystems at different scales. Use mathematical representations to support and revise explanations based on evidence about factors affecting biodiversity and populations in ecosystems of different scales.
meta_desc: Free high school biology worksheets on populations (NGSS HS-LS2-1, HS-LS2-2): population change, density, exponential and logistic growth, carrying capacity and mark-recapture. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Populations grow until limits stop them.
key_sub: The carrying capacity is the largest population the environment can support.
body_html:
How to think about it

Populations grow until limits stop them.

  • Change = (births + immigration) − (deaths + emigration).
  • With unlimited resources: exponential (J-curve). With limits: logistic (S-curve) up to the carrying capacity.
  • Density-dependent limits (food, disease, predators) grow stronger when crowded; density-independent ones (fire, flood) do not.
Example

500 rabbits; 120 births, 80 deaths, 10 in, 20 out. Next year?

(120 + 10) − (80 + 20) = 30

Answer: 530

Example

Mark 40, catch 50, 10 marked. N?

40 × 50 ÷ 10

Answer: 200

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a population keeps growing forever.
  • Calling a flood density-dependent. It affects any population size.
  • Multiplying all three numbers in mark-recapture.

faq.a: The largest population an environment can support over time, set by food, water, space and other limits.

faq.q: What is the difference between exponential and logistic growth?
faq.a: Exponential growth speeds up without limit (J-curve). Logistic growth slows and levels off at the carrying capacity (S-curve).
Mark some animals, release them, catch a second sample and use N = marked × caught ÷ recaptured.
